episode_thesis: Drew, Seykota's first apprentice, argues Seykota was a price-only discretionary trader, not the systematic trader Market Wizards implied, and that the transferable lessons are psychological and about sizing: fit style to temperament, bet bigger than feels comfortable but not to ruin, scale size with equity without extra drawdown cuts, and do not tinker in drawdowns.

speakers.name: Dave Drew
speakers.role: Systematic trader and fund manager; Seykota's first living apprentice (c. 1990-91)
speakers.speaker_note: Caption speaker labels are mixed; the closed-vs-open equity reasoning and the 1m->500k->250k example were said by the host Seibert (ledger corrections applied), Drew agreeing. Drew's own investor-fund practice (backtest everything, follow algorithms) is from ledger claims C02-X1/C04-X1.

worldview_premises.premise: Seykota is a technical discretionary trader on price only, not a systematic one; the Market Wizards picture of a computerised systematic trader is wrong. His software only displayed charts.
worldview_premises.support: Six months living and travelling with him.

worldview_premises.premise: Seykota's skill is intuitive and cannot be programmed or taught directly; it is passed on by observation (Jade master story).
worldview_premises.support: Anecdotes: hand-drawn Bund bar that came true; apprenticeship by hanging out.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets bring out hidden psychological problems, so unresolved psychology causes self-sabotage; self-limiting beliefs (not feeling worthy) hold traders back.
worldview_premises.support: Seykota's teaching and group sessions; cookie story.

worldview_premises.premise: A trading style must fit the trader's psychology; a person who cannot follow a computerised system will tinker with it even if it is excellent, and vice versa.
worldview_premises.support: Own 15-month discretionary experiment ended with a psychiatrist.

worldview_premises.premise: Trading with meaningful size is needed to learn about oneself because token amounts create no emotional stakes.

There is an optimal bet size for a system with a known edge, larger than most people will use; too large and ruin risk soars, too small and returns are low. Because edge is unstable over time, optimal size is only a rule of thumb.
worldview_premises.support: Article on heat distribution co-written with Seykota; Seykota's own extreme drawdowns.

worldview_premises.premise: No institution would back Seykota because his equity swings are huge; his aim was maximum profit, not controlled risk.
Drawdown behaviour is one of the biggest determinants of long-run success; confidence in solid research is what keeps a systematic trader on the rules.
worldview_premises.support: Own experience losing money for investors while following his system.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why tinkering in a drawdown and drawdown-reduction rules damage results

steps.to: Trader doubts system and alters it
steps.why: Pain makes people read 'something is wrong'.

steps.from: Risk is cut after losses (drawdown reduction rule)
steps.to: Too little risk to recover; system may stay underwater indefinitely
steps.why: Recovery needs normal bet size; cutting also distorts the system's statistics.

steps.from: Bet size scaled to current equity both up and down
steps.to: Constant fractional risk, lower ruin risk than scaling up only
steps.why: Scaling only upward leaves ruin risk higher after gains.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Experience and reasoning; no data offered.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated, except 'unless you are sure something is actually broken'.

steps.to: Trader tinkers with or abandons the method
steps.why: Cannot stick to rules that clash with temperament.

steps.from: Drew pretends to be Seykota with discretion
steps.to: 300% return in 15 months but breakdown and psychiatrist

mechanism_chains.evidence: Single personal case (300% vs systems' 20%); not repeatable evidence.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: When trader temperament cannot support the style.

decision_process.practice: Own funds: backtest every rule before implementing, then follow the algorithms strictly.
decision_process.why: Investors need a statistical record; discretionary has none.

decision_process.practice: Bet size proportional to current equity (2x at 2 million), rising and falling; no extra drawdown cut.
decision_process.why: Avoid ruin and avoid staying underwater.

decision_process.practice: Size off closed-trade equity (after stops), not open-trade equity; open-equity sizing 'never works really'.
decision_process.why: Closed equity is more stable (reasoning added by host).

decision_process.practice: Do not change a system during a drawdown unless sure something is broken; let the statistics play out.
Discretionary trading kept to a disclosed personal account, never offered to investors.
Daily end-of-day data cleaning of bad prints before analysis.
decision_process.why: Raw downloads had many bad data points.

speakers.evidence_style: Personal anecdote and apprenticeship stories; own track-record comparison; reasoning about sizing; no backtests shown in this episode.

speakers.name: Ed Seykota (relayed by Drew)
speakers.role: Discretionary technical trader; subject of Drew's account
speakers.speaker_note: Never speaks; every statement is Drew's second-hand report. Not a speaker in the transcript but his views are the topic, so mapped separately and flagged.

worldview_premises.premise: Price-only technical discretionary trading, ignoring news, earns more than systematic trading.
Maximum return requires betting big and tolerating very high heat; most people cannot, and overshooting wipes you out.
worldview_premises.support: His own drawdowns (up to ~50% in a day).

worldview_premises.premise: Unresolved psychology and unworthiness limit success.

decision_process.practice: About ten minutes on end-of-day charts, pick approximate entry and stop for next day; sacrosanct rules: cut losses short, let profits ride, diversify.
No memory of recent losses; act correctly each day.

speakers.name: Moritz Seibert
speakers.speaker_note: Host who states views on sizing (ledger corrections C07-1, C07-2).

worldview_premises.premise: Open-trade equity includes volatile open profits and invites over-risking; closed-trade equity is a stable step function and a better sizing base.
After a 50% drawdown, size on the reduced base but do not cut further; extra de-risking leaves too little risk to recover and distorts the system's statistics.

decision_process.practice: Size on current (closed-trade) equity after a drawdown, no additional reduction.
decision_process.why: Preserve the ability to recover and system statistics.

positions.speaker: Ed Seykota (via Drew)
positions.position: Technical discretionary trading on price earns more than systematic.

positions.speaker: Dave Drew
positions.position: Systematic and backtested is the only responsible approach for investors; discretionary did not fit his psychology.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Drew's 300% vs 20% comparison is a single 15-month personal account vs investor systems, different risk levels; Drew nonetheless prefers systems.
Optimal bet size is conceded to be unstable because edge varies, yet the advice is to size above what most would use; no number or method given.
Seykota 'lost no more than 50% in a day' is an unverifiable second-hand anecdote.
Sizing off closed equity: the reason given is the host's, not Drew's.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) None: no market view or forward indicator; the episode is about process, psychology and sizing.
reader_inferences: (reader) Equity-proportional sizing with no extra drawdown reduction is a constant-fraction (Kelly-like) rule; its tolerance of deep heat depends on the fraction chosen, which was not specified.
(reader) The 300% discretionary result would not be evidence of edge given one account, 15 months and unknown leverage.

added_claims.claim: Drew relays Seykota's answer on his biggest drawdown: he does not think he lost more than 50% in a day, i.e. extreme heat is part of his return.
